# THE VARAHA OF KALINGA

### REVISITING ODIA MANHOOD ON THE CORONATION DAY OF GAJAPATI KAPILENDRADEVA

[](https://substack.com/@ekavali)

> “*When the world was sinking under the mud and when the civilization
> was vanishing through the atrocities of the ‘Mlechchas’, Gajapati
> Kapilendra appeared on the scene and saved the world and acted like
> the Kalki and the Boar incarnation of Vishnu*”-

-***Gopinathpur inscription of Gopinath Mahapatra*** (general of Gajapati Kapilendradeva)

The 29th of June, marks one of the most electric dates in Odisha’s history—the Coronation Day of Gajapati Kapilendradeva (1435 CE). This isn’t just a random date for history textbooks; it is a blueprint for what authentic Odia manhood and leadership could possibly mean.

When we talk about “masculinity” or “manhood” today, the conversation often gets trapped between toxic bravado and fragile passivity. Yet, nearly six centuries ago on this very soil, a man rose from the ranks of a general or, if one accepts the account of the Jagannath Temple chronicle, the Madala Panji, from the common populace to completely redefine power. His pauruṣa was not exactly a birthright. Although he belonged to the family of Jagesvara Nayaka (possibly a general or a provincial governor), his pauruṣa(manhood) was equally shaped in the fire of meritocracy.Before ascending the throne, the Odia man had to establish himself as an accomplished commander under his predecessor ie the ruler of Eastern Ganga dynasty. Kapilendradeva first secured the confidence of influential nobles and generals before eventually staging a successful coup. Thereafter, he suppressed internal rebellions and expanded the Gajapati Empire across nearly one-third of the Indian subcontinent through a combination of competent generals, strategic patience, tactical alliances and the resolute application of daṇḍa (punitive authority) whenever necessary. At the same time, the Kaifiyats(local historical records of towns and villages primarily from the Deccan and South India ) from Andhra Pradesh portray him as a generous and righteous ruler, suggesting that military success and ethical kingship were not perceived as mutually exclusive.

Equally remarkable is the paradox evident in his inscriptions. Despite being celebrated in royal epigraphy through almost divine imagery as scion of Solar clan & the One who is adorned with qualities of Rama, Kapilendradeva repeatedly described himself as the Rauta and servant of Lord Jagannath. One may dismiss this as a conventional expression of kṣatriya devotion towards one’s Kuladevatā. Yet the final known inscription of Kapilendradeva appears to reveal a far more personal dimension. He perhaps faced a dynastic succession dispute and internal discontent within an expanding empire and still the Emperor’s language reflects not triumphalism but profound surrender before Lord Jagannath. Strength and humility thus coexisted rather than contradicted one another. A legitimate question arises: can the experience of a king be taken to represent the ideals of an entire society? The careers of his distinguished commanders—Gopinath Mahapatra, Ganadeva Routray, Damodar Pattnaik, Narendra Mahapatra, Kashi Mahapatra—as well as those of his son Hamvira and nephew Raghudeva, suggest that these values might not be confined to the Emperor alone. They appear to represent a wider political and military culture that valued competence, loyalty and disciplined service.

But what of the ordinary Odia man? The historical record offers fewer examples. Nevertheless, the life of a certain Sidheswar Parida, better known as Sarala Das, remains particularly instructive. Tradition holds that after serving as a soldier under Kapilendradeva, he devoted himself to literary pursuits. Although he may not have received formal scholastic training, his intellectual curiosity and personal effort culminated in the composition of the Sarala Mahabharata, one of the most celebrated regional renderings of the epic. This perhaps indicates pauruṣa was not confined to martial excellence alone, it also embraced self-cultivation and the pursuit of knowledge.

So what was the ideal ‘medieval Odia’ manhood? It is not performative dominance but earned authority which was not an inherited privilege but a demonstrated capability. It prizes strategic patience over impulsive aggression, collective achievement over individual glory. Equally striking is its openness to transformation. A soldier could become a poet, a military commander could become an empire-builder, an emperor could still call himself the servant of Jagannath. Identity was defined less by birth and more by conduct, less by status than by one’s ability to cultivate śakti, yukti and bhakti together. Perhaps that is why Odia pauruṣa was not likely a cult of machismo. In the broader historiography of masculinity, the medieval Odia archetype offers an alternative to many conventional models that equate manhood primarily with dominance and the assertion of individual power. Instead, medieval Odia pauruṣa appears to be based upon a distinctive Indic ideal, where the martial vigour of the soldier was balanced by the humility of the devotee. Power was not viewed as an end in itself but derived its legitimacy through service to a higher moral and cosmic order. In this synthesis, physical strength was transformed from mere machismo into an instrument for safeguarding society and civilization. The Odia masculine ideal was not centred on the lone hero but on the creation of a disciplined brotherhood capable of defending and renewing civilization. Kapilendradeva’s achievements rested on trusted commanders and administrators, while the Gopinathpur inscription remembers him as a restorer of a world descending into chaos. Masculinity thus lay in safeguarding society through collective competence rather than individual bravado.

Today, the modern Odia male is often caricatured as quiet, unassertive, or politically timid. Yet history records a fiercely different archetype, making the story of Gajapati Kapilendradeva the ultimate lesson in reclaiming authentic Paurusha.
